periods.activity_title: Why the Map Changed: Invasions and the Making of the Delhi Sultanate
periods.section_anchor: Rise and Fall of the Delhi Sultanate
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Outline political map of India (blank, one per pair)
Coloured pencils
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn timeline on board: five Sultanate dynasties (Mamluk to Lodi) with approximate dates

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's organising question: 'What forces reshaped India's political map between the 11th and 17th centuries?' Students read the opening paragraph of the chapter summary aloud and identify three stated motivations for the Turkic-Afghan invasions — India's reputed riches, territorial ambitions, and religious motivations — writing them as a quick individual list.

Teacher draws the five-dynasty timeline on the board (Mamluks, Khiljis, Tughlaqs, Sayyids, Lodis) and presents four specific events as case studies of the Sultanate's instability: Prithviraj Chauhan's defeat in 1192, Ala-ud-din Khilji's southern campaigns through Malik Kafur, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's capital-shift to Daulatabad and copper-currency experiment, and Timur's 1398 raid. For each event, teacher asks: 'What did this change — politically, economically, or socially?' Students annotate their timeline.

Pairs receive blank outline maps. Using the four case studies, they shade the approximate Sultanate territory at its peak under Ala-ud-din Khilji, mark Delhi and Daulatabad, and write a two-sentence caption explaining how Muhammad bin Tughlaq's decisions contributed to political and economic decline. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'What is the difference between expanding an empire and governing it effectively?'

Pairs share captions. Teacher consolidates: the Sultanate's five-dynasty arc shows that military expansion without stable governance produces its own decline — the jizya, violent successions, and Timur's raid are all consequences of this structural weakness. Students record one 'change' and one 'consequence' from the session in their notebooks.

periods.section_context: Five Turkic-Afghan dynasties, Khilji campaigns, Tughlaq capital-shift, Timur's raid
periods.teacher_notes: Open by anchoring to the chapter title itself — 'reshaping' implies both gain and loss, which sets up everything that follows. A common confusion is treating all five dynasties as a single continuous power; stress that each dynasty came to power through internal conflict, not smooth succession. The map activity makes the territorial argument concrete before students encounter the Vijayanagara and Mughal sections.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how political instability and policy failures produce cascading social and economic consequences.

periods.activity_title: Holding the Line: Kingdoms That Resisted the Delhi Sultanate
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Printed or projected map showing Eastern Ganga, Hoysala, and Mewar territories
Structured comparison worksheet (three columns: Kingdom | Method of Resistance | Outcome)
periods.visual_aids: Map showing approximate territories of Eastern Gangas (Kalinga/Odisha-Bengal-Andhra), Hoysalas (south), Mewar (northwest), and Bahmani Sultanate (Deccan)

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects the regional map and asks students to locate three areas not under Sultanate control: Kalinga in the east, the Hoysala kingdom in the south, and Mewar in the northwest. Students identify these on their own maps and write one question they want to answer: 'How did these kingdoms survive while the Sultanate was at its peak?'

Teacher presents three resistance cases in sequence. (1) Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I defeated the Sultanate's Bengal governor in the mid-13th century and built the Konark Surya temple to commemorate the victory. (2) The Musunuri Nayakas formed a confederacy of over 75 Telugu chieftains that expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq's forces from Warangal around 1330–1336. (3) Rana Kumbha of Mewar repelled invasions from the Delhi Sultanate and regional sultanates in the 15th century. For each case, teacher asks: 'What made this resistance possible — geography, unity, military power, or timing?'

Students complete the comparison worksheet, filling in the method of resistance and outcome for each kingdom. Then they write one analytical sentence answering: 'What do these three cases suggest about the limits of the Sultanate's power?' Teacher circulates and challenges superficial answers — pushing from 'they were strong' to identifying specific structural factors such as confederacy-building or geography.

Whole-class share-out of analytical sentences. Teacher draws attention to the Hoysalas: they resisted multiple Sultanate attacks but eventually weakened and were absorbed into the rising Vijayanagara Empire — raising the question of what happens when a resistant kingdom itself declines. Teacher introduces the Bahmani Sultanate briefly as the Deccan power that emerged in the mid-14th century, setting up the next section.

periods.section_context: Eastern Gangas, Musunuri Nayakas confederacy, Hoysalas, Rana Kumbha, Konark temple
periods.teacher_notes: The Konark temple is an important anchor here — it is simultaneously a military commemoration and a cultural achievement, which connects political resistance to cultural production. Students often treat the Hoysalas and Eastern Gangas as minor footnotes; the comparison worksheet forces equal analytical attention on all three. The Hoysalas' eventual absorption sets up the Vijayanagara Empire's emergence organically.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the structural factors — geographic, political, and organisational — that enabled communities to sustain resistance against expansionist powers.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how regional kingdoms shaped the limits of imperial expansion through organised resistance.

periods.activity_title: Building a Southern Power: The Vijayanagara Empire
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Outline map of peninsular India
Short paragraph extract about Harihara and Bukka's break from Tughlaq authority (from chapter summary)
periods.visual_aids: Sketch map on board: Vijayanagara core territory, Bahmani Sultanate, five Deccan Sultanates, and Gajapati rulers of Odisha

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the Tughlaq period's instability — the capital-shift, currency failure, and Warangal expulsion — and asks: 'What political vacuum did that instability create in the south?' Students predict in pairs, then teacher introduces Harihara and Bukka as administrators under Muhammad bin Tughlaq who broke away and founded what grew into the Vijayanagara Empire.

Teacher draws the sketch map showing Vijayanagara's position between the Bahmani Sultanate to the north and the Gajapati rulers of Odisha to the northeast. Students label their own outline maps. Teacher then explains: the Bahmani Sultanate itself eventually fragmented into five Deccan Sultanates — Bijapur, Golconda, Berar, Ahmednagar, and Bidar. Students list all five and mark the general Deccan zone on their maps. Discussion question: 'What does it tell us about power in the Deccan that Vijayanagara's major rival itself broke into five pieces?'

Students write a structured paragraph (four to five sentences) responding to: 'How did the political fragmentation of the Deccan shape the rise and position of the Vijayanagara Empire?' They must use at least three specific names — Harihara/Bukka, the Bahmani Sultanate, and one of the five Deccan Sultanates — and explain a cause-effect relationship, not just list facts.

Two or three students read their paragraphs aloud. Teacher evaluates whether cause-effect reasoning is present or whether students listed facts without connecting them. Teacher closes by noting that Vijayanagara became a 'significant political and cultural force'.

periods.section_context: Harihara and Bukka's founding, Bahmani Sultanate, five Deccan Sultanates, Gajapati rulers
periods.teacher_notes: The key analytical move is connecting Tughlaq instability to Vijayanagara's founding — two brothers leaving Tughlaq service is not coincidence but consequence. Students often confuse the Bahmani Sultanate with the five Deccan Sultanates it became; the map helps distinguish the original rival from its successors. Keeping the Gajapati rulers on the map prevents the narrative from treating Vijayanagara as isolated from eastern India.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how imperial fragmentation creates political space for new powers to emerge and consolidate.

periods.activity_title: Peak and Fall: Krishnadevaraya and Vijayanagara's Legacy
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Short translated extract from Domingo Paes' travel account (teacher-prepared, 4–5 sentences)
Source analysis worksheet: two columns — 'What the source says' | 'What it reveals about Vijayanagara'
periods.visual_aids: Image of the Vitthala temple at Hampi (projected or in textbook)

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the Domingo Paes extract. Students read it individually and write one sentence: 'What kind of source is this, and what can it reliably tell us about Vijayanagara?' Teacher clarifies: a Portuguese traveller's first-hand account is a primary source but carries the observer's own perspective and limitations.

Teacher presents Krishnadevaraya's profile: military expansion over the Deccan, patronage of poets and scholars in Sanskrit, Telugu, and Kannada, composition of the Telugu epic Amuktamalyada, and grants to Tirupati and the Vitthala temple. Students fill the source analysis worksheet using the Paes extract: left column records specific claims Paes makes (prosperity, population, city scale); right column identifies what each claim reveals about the empire's economic and political condition under Krishnadevaraya.

Teacher then presents the empire's decline: Krishnadevaraya's death in 1529, and the 1565 Battle of Talikota where a coalition of Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara forces, sacking and destroying the capital. The empire fragmented under Nayakas — former military governors — and ended in the mid-17th century. Students answer: 'Was Talikota inevitable, or did specific decisions after 1529 cause the decline? Identify one factor from each side of this argument.'

Small groups share their arguments for and against inevitability. Teacher consolidates: the chapter presents Vijayanagara as both a political and cultural peak, and its fall as evidence that even well-resourced empires are vulnerable to coalition threats. The Nayaka fragmentation mirrors the Bahmani→five Sultanates pattern from the previous unit, pointing to a recurring structure in Deccan political history.

periods.section_context: Krishnadevaraya's patronage, Amuktamalyada, Paes account, Battle of Talikota, Nayakas
periods.teacher_notes: The Domingo Paes extract is central to developing source-interpretation skills — students often take traveller accounts at face value; push them to ask what Paes could not have seen or might have exaggerated. Amuktamalyada is frequently mispronounced; write it on the board phonetically. The peak-then-fall structure mirrors the Delhi Sultanate arc, and pointing that out explicitly builds analytical pattern-recognition.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how a political and cultural peak coexists with structural vulnerabilities that precipitate an empire's collapse.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect and interpret multiple sources of information (primary and secondary).
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extract and critically assess information from a traveller's primary account to draw inferences about a historical society.

periods.activity_title: Gunpowder and Autobiography: Babur and the Mughal Founding
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Two short translated passages from the Baburnama (teacher-prepared): one on Babur's military tactics, one on his impressions of India
Source analysis worksheet
periods.visual_aids: Timeline on board: Babur (1526 Panipat I) → Humayun → Sher Shah Suri interlude → Humayun's reconquest → Himu defeated at Panipat II (1556)

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the timeline and introduces Babur as a Turkic-Mongol ruler descended from Timur, driven from Samarkand. Teacher asks: 'Timur raided India in 1398 and left. Why did Babur, also from Timur's line, stay and build an empire?' Students discuss in pairs and share predictions — teacher does not confirm yet.

Students read both Baburnama passages. Using the source analysis worksheet, they record: (1) what the military-tactics passage reveals about why Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 — specifically the role of gunpowder and field artillery, and (2) what the India-impressions passage reveals about Babur's attitude toward the territory he had conquered. Teacher asks: 'Does the Baburnama give you a flattering or complicated picture of Babur? What does it reveal about the relationship between cultural sophistication and military ruthlessness?'

Teacher presents the succession crisis: Humayun's struggles, Sher Shah Suri's takeover of north India, Humayun's reconquest, and then Himu's brief capture of Delhi before Akbar's forces defeated him at the Second Battle of Panipat. Students create a brief cause-effect chain (four boxes, arrows between them) showing how the Mughal Empire nearly collapsed and was re-established within thirty years of Babur's victory.

Pairs share cause-effect chains and compare links. Teacher consolidates: the Baburnama is the first named autobiography in this chapter — it is both a historical source and a piece of literature, which is unusual for rulers of this era. Students record: 'What does the existence of the Baburnama tell us about Babur beyond what a chronicle of battles would tell?'

periods.section_context: Babur, First Panipat 1526, Baburnama, Humayun, Sher Shah Suri, Himu, Second Panipat
periods.teacher_notes: The Baburnama is important as a primary source that complicates the simple 'invader' narrative — Babur describes India with both admiration and condescension, which is itself historically significant. Students often conflate the two Battles of Panipat; the timeline on the board should clearly separate them by date and combatants. Sher Shah Suri's interlude is worth dwelling on briefly — it produced significant administrative reforms that Akbar later built on.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect and interpret multiple sources of information (primary and secondary).
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret an autobiographical primary source to identify the author's perspective and distinguish it from neutral historical record.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the sequence of political disruptions that shaped the early Mughal Empire's consolidation.

periods.activity_title: Conquest and Tolerance: Akbar's Empire-Building Strategies
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Two-column graphic organiser: 'Military/Coercive Strategies' | 'Political/Tolerant Strategies'
Short passage from Ain-i-Akbari (teacher-prepared, 3–4 sentences on sulh-i-kul)
periods.visual_aids: Portrait of Akbar's court at Fatehpur Sikri (projected or textbook illustration)

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents a two-part provocation: 'Akbar ordered the massacre of 30,000 civilians at Chittorgarh. He also abolished the jizya and founded a house of translation. Can both of these be true of the same ruler?' Students write a two-sentence initial response before any further input.

Teacher presents Akbar's strategies systematically. Students fill the graphic organiser: Military/Coercive column — Chittorgarh siege and massacre, military conquest of Rajput kingdoms. Political/Tolerant column — abolition of jizya, marriage alliances with Rajput kingdoms, appointment of Hindu officials, sulh-i-kul doctrine, interfaith dialogues, translation of the Mahabharata, Ramayana, Bhagavad Gita, and Panchatantra into Persian at Fatehpur Sikri. Students read the Ain-i-Akbari passage on sulh-i-kul and add it to the appropriate column.

Students write a paragraph (five to six sentences) arguing: 'Were Akbar's tolerant policies a genuine change in values, or were they strategic political tools — or both?' They must cite at least two specific policies and explain the reasoning behind their position. Teacher circulates and challenges students who treat this as a simple either/or: 'Can a strategy also reflect genuine values?'

Three students share paragraphs representing different positions. Class votes on the most persuasive argument — not the 'correct' one — and discusses what additional evidence would strengthen each position. Teacher notes: Akbar's reign of nearly 50 years (1556–1605) is the longest in this chapter, and the empire's stability under Jahangir and Shah Jahan is partly a consequence of the administrative and political foundations he built.

periods.section_context: Chittorgarh siege, jizya abolition, Rajput alliances, sulh-i-kul, Fatehpur Sikri translations
periods.teacher_notes: The tension between Akbar's violence at Chittorgarh and his later tolerance is the unit's analytical engine — students who flatten him into either 'tolerant emperor' or 'brutal conqueror' are missing the chapter's complexity. The Ain-i-Akbari passage is important here because it is a source produced by Akbar's court, which raises questions about reliability. The translation project at Fatehpur Sikri connects to the C-7.3 tradition of inclusion and is worth treating as more than a cultural footnote.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how a ruler's shifting strategies — from coercion to accommodation — reshape political and social relations across an empire.

competency_edges.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of inclusion across communities and social groups.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate specific policies and doctrines as evidence of — or departures from — traditions of inclusion in governance.

periods.activity_title: Expansion and Decline: Aurangzeb's Reign and Its Consequences
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Short extract from Aurangzeb's 1669 edict ordering temple demolitions (teacher-prepared summary, 3–4 sentences)
Cause-consequence map template (single large box at top for decision; arrows leading to three consequence boxes)
periods.visual_aids: Map showing Mughal Empire at greatest extent under Aurangzeb versus Akbar's empire

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the map comparing Mughal extent under Akbar and under Aurangzeb. Students observe: Aurangzeb's empire is larger. Teacher asks: 'If the empire reached its greatest size under Aurangzeb, why did it collapse so quickly after his death in 1707?' Students write a one-sentence prediction.

Teacher presents Aurangzeb's profile in two parts. Part 1 — seizure of power: defeated and executed Dara Shikoh, imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort, removed other brothers, crowned himself in 1658. Part 2 — policies: banned music and dance at court, reimposed jizya and pilgrimage tax, and in 1669 ordered demolition of Hindu and Jain temples and Sikh gurudwaras including those at Varanasi, Mathura, and Somnath. Students read the edict extract and note: 'What does the language of this edict tell us about the reasoning Aurangzeb used to justify these orders?'

Students complete the cause-consequence map for Aurangzeb's 25-year Deccan wars: they place 'Prolonged Deccan military campaigns' in the top box and identify three consequences — treasury depletion, administrative strain, rapid post-1707 decline. They then add a second map for the religious policy decisions and identify three consequences — rebellions, Rajput resistance, Sikh-Mughal conflict escalation.

Pairs compare maps. Teacher asks: 'Which set of consequences — from military overreach or from religious policy — was more damaging to the empire's long-term survival? Is it possible to separate the two?' Students record a two-sentence response. Teacher notes that the post-1707 fragmentation sets the stage for the Maratha rise and eventual British entry.

periods.section_context: Aurangzeb's seizure of power, jizya reimposition, 1669 demolition edict, Deccan wars, 1707 decline
periods.teacher_notes: The 1669 edict is a primary source document that students should approach analytically — what does the edict's language reveal about Aurangzeb's stated justifications? A common confusion is treating Aurangzeb's territorial expansion as evidence of a strong empire; the cause-consequence map forces students to see expansion and overextension as two sides of the same phenomenon. Aurangzeb's deathbed letters acknowledging failure are mentioned in the chapter and could be referenced as a secondary evidence point if time allows.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct causal chains linking a ruler's military and policy decisions to the structural decline of an empire.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify how state religious policies generate or intensify communal conflict and its political consequences.

periods.activity_title: Many Forms of Resistance: Jats, Tribal Communities, and Rani Durgavati
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Brief reading on Rani Durgavati (from chapter summary, teacher-prepared paragraph)
Structured discussion prompt cards (one per group of four)
periods.visual_aids: Sketch map indicating Garha kingdom (central India), Jat regions (north), and approximate territories of Bhils, Gonds, Santhals, and Kochs

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects the sketch map and introduces three categories of Mughal resistance: (1) peasant communities — Jat uprisings in the 17th century against oppressive administration; (2) tribal groups — Bhils, Gonds, Santhals, and Kochs fighting annexation and taxation; (3) regional queens — Rani Durgavati of the Garha kingdom. Students identify which category they find most surprising and briefly explain why.

Students read the Rani Durgavati paragraph. Teacher presents the three resistance categories in more depth: Jat peasants organised against Mughal administration (not a foreign power, but the empire they lived under); tribal groups in forested and hilly regions maintained varying degrees of independence through geography and knowledge of terrain; Rani Durgavati ruled wisely, maintained a substantial army, and fell fighting Akbar's forces in 1564 rather than surrender. Discussion question on prompt cards: 'What do these three forms of resistance have in common, and how are they different in motivation, method, and outcome?'

Groups of four discuss using the prompt card. Each group must identify: one shared factor across all three forms of resistance, one factor unique to Rani Durgavati's case, and one factor that explains why tribal groups could sustain independence even when others could not. Groups write their three answers on a shared piece of paper.

Groups share their unique-factor answers. Teacher consolidates: resistance to the Mughals was not confined to powerful kings or armies — peasants, tribal communities, and regional rulers all pushed back for different reasons. The chapter presents Rani Durgavati specifically as a 'symbol of regional resistance,' and students should ask: what makes a historical figure a symbol rather than simply a participant?

periods.section_context: Jat peasant uprisings, Bhils, Gonds, Santhals, Kochs, Rani Durgavati of Garha kingdom
periods.teacher_notes: Students often default to treating resistance as military; the Jat and tribal cases push them toward economic and territorial motivations that are just as analytically important. Rani Durgavati's story is frequently reduced to a heroic death narrative — the question about what makes someone a 'symbol' prevents that flattening. The tribal groups' use of geography and terrain connects forward to the Ahoms unit, so noting that link here prepares the ground.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare the motivations and methods of diverse resisting communities to identify patterns in how groups contest imperial authority.

periods.activity_title: Swords and Alliances: The Rajputs and the Ahoms
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Outline map showing Mewar, Marwar, Aravalli hills, and Brahmaputra Valley
Two-column note-maker: Rajputs | Ahoms
periods.visual_aids: Timeline strip: Rana Sanga defeated by Babur (Khanwa) → Maharana Pratap (Haldighati 1576) → Durga Das Rathore rebellion under Aurangzeb; parallel track: Ahoms in Brahmaputra Valley, Battle of Saraighat 1671

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the two-track timeline and asks students to consider: 'Both the Rajputs and the Ahoms resisted Mughal expansion for over a century. What might explain such sustained resistance?' Students write two hypotheses.

Teacher presents the Rajput track: Rana Sanga unified several clans but was defeated by Babur at Khanwa; Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused Mughal suzerainty and fought at Haldighati in 1576, then waged years of guerrilla warfare from the Aravalli hills with Bhil community support; during Aurangzeb's reign, Durga Das Rathore of Marwar kept Mughal authority limited in Rajasthan; some Rajput states eventually allied with the Mughals through marriage and diplomacy. Teacher asks: 'Is allying with the Mughals a form of defeat or a form of political strategy?'

Teacher presents the Ahom track: migrated from present-day Myanmar in the 13th century to the Brahmaputra Valley; resisted both Sultanate and Mughal expansion using the paik system (every able-bodied man provides labour or military service in exchange for land rights); when Aurangzeb's forces briefly captured Garhgaon, the Ahoms used terrain knowledge — forests, hills, rivers — and guerrilla tactics; the Battle of Saraighat in 1671, led by Lachit Borphukan, saw 10,000 Ahom soldiers defeat a Mughal force of 30,000. Students fill the two-column note-maker, identifying what unique resource or strategy each group relied on.

Students answer in writing: 'Compare the Rajput and Ahom strategies for maintaining independence. What does each case reveal about the different forms that resistance can take?' Teacher consolidates: both groups used knowledge of their own terrain, but the Ahoms also had a structural military-economic system (paik) that the Rajputs did not. The Rajputs' eventual partial accommodation with the Mughals versus the Ahoms' near-total independence points to how geography and institutional design shape outcomes.

periods.section_context: Rana Sanga, Maharana Pratap, Haldighati, Durga Das Rathore, paik system, Lachit Borphukan, Saraighat
periods.teacher_notes: The paik system is the Ahoms unit's most analytically distinctive feature — it is an institutional design that converts land rights into military capacity, which is different from both the Mughal mansabdari and the Rajput clan structure. Students often treat Haldighati as a defeat for Maharana Pratap; the chapter emphasises his subsequent guerrilla warfare as the more significant achievement. The Bhil community's support for Maharana Pratap connects back to the tribal resistance unit and rewards explicit cross-reference.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare contrasting strategies of sustained resistance — martial tradition, institutional design, terrain knowledge — and evaluate their effectiveness across different political contexts.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how specific institutional and geographic factors determined the degree of independence regional powers maintained against a dominant empire.

periods.activity_title: Faith, Persecution, and the Khalsa: The Rise of the Sikhs
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Short passage from the chapter on Guru Nanak's message (teacher-prepared, 3–4 sentences)
Structured timeline worksheet: six events from Guru Nanak's founding to Maharaja Ranjit Singh
periods.visual_aids: Timeline on board: Guru Nanak (15th century) → Guru Arjan's death under Jahangir → Guru Hargobind's martial turn → Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution (1675) → Khalsa founding (1699) → Maharaja Ranjit Singh (early 19th century)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Guru Nanak passage aloud — equality, compassion, oneness of God — and asks: 'How does a community founded on these values come to organise a martial brotherhood within two centuries?' Students predict the trigger in pairs.

Teacher walks through the timeline: Guru Nanak founded Sikhism in 15th-century Punjab; Emperor Jahangir tortured Guru Arjan to death, prompting Guru Hargobind to introduce martial training and form a Sikh army; in 1675 Guru Tegh Bahadur stood against Aurangzeb's religious persecution on behalf of Kashmiri Pandits and was publicly beheaded in Delhi; Guru Gobind Singh responded by founding the Khalsa in 1699 — a martial brotherhood committed to justice, equality, and defence of faith. Students fill the timeline worksheet with the trigger, response, and outcome for each transition.

Students answer the analytical question: 'The Khalsa was founded in response to persecution, but it also carried Guru Nanak's original values of equality and justice. How did the founding of the Khalsa transform those values rather than abandon them?' Students write four to five sentences, using specific events from the timeline as evidence.

Three students share responses. Teacher consolidates: the Sikh-Mughal conflict is not simply a religious war — it begins with the Mughal state's targeting of a community and escalates through specific, nameable acts of persecution. The eventual unification under Maharaja Ranjit Singh and resistance to British expansion shows the Sikh Empire as a lasting political consequence of this trajectory. Teacher asks students to note: 'What does Guru Tegh Bahadur's defence of Kashmiri Pandits suggest about how the Khalsa understood the principle of justice?'

periods.section_context: Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan's death, Guru Hargobind, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Khalsa 1699, Ranjit Singh
periods.teacher_notes: Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution is the pivot point of this unit — he died defending a community not his own, which is the chapter's clearest statement of the inclusion tradition. Students sometimes confuse the Khalsa's martial identity with aggression; the founding principles (justice, equality, defence of faith) need to be held alongside the military dimension. The transition from a community founded on Nanak's non-violent message to one with a standing army is the unit's intellectual core and should not be rushed.

periods.activity_title: How Empires Were Run: The Delhi Sultanate's Administrative System
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Graphic organiser: 'Delhi Sultanate Administration' with fields for central authority, iqta system, tax collection, and impact on peasantry
Short passage on the iqta system (from chapter summary, teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Diagram on board: Sultan → Council of Ministers → Iqtadars (non-hereditary) → Tax collection → Treasury (for army funding) → Peasantry bears burden

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the administrative diagram and poses the question: 'The iqta system gave nobles land — but it was not hereditary. Why does that distinction matter for how power was distributed?' Students discuss in pairs and record their reasoning.

Teacher presents the Delhi Sultanate's administrative structure: the sultan as absolute political and military authority assisted by a council of ministers; the iqta system assigning territories to iqtadars to collect taxes primarily for army funding; the non-hereditary nature of posts creating a network of local administrators who owed their position to the sultan rather than to birth right. Students fill the graphic organiser, noting what each layer of the system was responsible for and what it depended on.

Students answer: 'The iqta system was designed to fund the army, but how did it shape the lives of people who were not nobles or soldiers? Use evidence from the chapter to support your argument.' Students must address the tax burden on the peasantry and connect it to the system's design, not just describe it as an outcome.

Three or four students share responses. Teacher consolidates: the non-hereditary character of the iqta system concentrated power with the sultan but created instability — iqtadars had incentive to extract maximum revenue before losing their position. This connects back to the Sultanate's political instability studied earlier: administrative design and political volatility reinforced each other. Students record: 'How does the design of the iqta system reflect the values and priorities of the Sultanate as a state?'

periods.section_context: Sultan's absolute authority, iqta system, iqtadars, non-hereditary posts, army funding, peasant tax burden
periods.teacher_notes: The non-hereditary nature of the iqta is the key analytical feature. Students often treat 'tax burden on peasantry' as a moral statement rather than an analytical one; push them to connect the system's structural incentives to that outcome. The diagram on the board should remain visible through the Mughal administration unit so students can compare directly.

periods.activity_title: Reforming the State: Akbar's Mughal Administrative Framework
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Comparison table worksheet: 'Delhi Sultanate Administration' vs 'Mughal Administration' — rows for central authority, military organisation, revenue system, provincial structure
Short passage on the mansabdari system (from chapter summary, teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Expanded diagram on board adding: Mughal track — Diwan, Mir Bakhshi, Khan-i-Saman, Sadr → 12 subahs → Mansabdars/Jagirdars → Todar Mal's land surveys

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns to the iqta system diagram from the Delhi Sultanate unit and asks: 'Akbar reorganised the Mughal administration. What problems from the Sultanate system might he have been trying to solve?' Students predict two or three problems, drawing on what they know of Sultanate instability.

Teacher presents the Mughal framework: specialised ministers at the centre — Diwan for finances, Mir Bakhshi for military, Khan-i-Saman for public works and agriculture, Sadr for justice and education; twelve provinces (subahs) with subdivisions; the mansabdari system where officers maintained specified troops and animals according to rank, paid through jagirs (land grants) and known as jagirdars; Todar Mal's systematic land surveys to improve revenue collection; and the chapter's note that non-Muslim officials remained a minority in senior posts. Students fill the comparison table.

Students write a structured comparison (five to six sentences): 'How did the Mughal administrative system address weaknesses in the Delhi Sultanate's system — and did it create new problems of its own?' They must use at least three named elements from each system and identify both what was improved and what remained problematic.

Pairs exchange written comparisons and annotate each other's work: underline one claim they agree with, circle one claim that needs more evidence. Teacher consolidates: the mansabdari system, like the iqta, was designed to give the emperor control over the military without a permanent standing army — but jagirdars, like iqtadars, had incentives to extract maximum revenue. Administrative reform does not necessarily solve structural incentive problems.

periods.section_context: Diwan, Mir Bakhshi, Khan-i-Saman, Sadr, 12 subahs, mansabdars, jagirdars, Todar Mal's surveys
periods.teacher_notes: The comparison with the iqta system is the analytical payoff of having taught unit 11 first — but this unit should name the concepts, not assume students remember the sequence. The mansabdari system's jagir mechanism is analogous to the iqta but with ranked obligations, which is a meaningful refinement. Todar Mal's land surveys are worth dwelling on as a data-driven reform — an early example of the state using empirical methods to improve governance, connecting to the chapter's broader Social Science methodology theme.

periods.activity_title: Lives Beneath the Empires: Economy, Trade, and Everyday Society
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Data card set (teacher-prepared): one card per institution — shreni, jati, hundi, temple economy, agrarian structure — each with three factual details
Structured writing frame for analytical paragraph
periods.visual_aids: Map of trade ports: Calicut, Surat, Mangalore, Hooghly — with arrows indicating export goods (textiles, weapons, utensils, ship-built goods) and import goods (luxury items, silk, horses)

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects the trade port map and asks: 'Political empires rose and fell between the 13th and 17th centuries. But trade from Calicut, Surat, Mangalore, and Hooghly continued. What economic institutions made this continuity possible despite political upheaval?' Students examine the map and write one hypothesis.

Each pair receives two data cards. Students read their cards and prepare to explain their institution to the class in two sentences. Teacher then leads a quick round: each pair explains their institution — shrenis (guilds organising artisans), jatis (professional communities), hundi (cross-border fund transfers without physical currency), temple economy (donated land, credit, maritime trade funding), agrarian structure (rulers extracted one-fifth to one-half of produce as land revenue). Teacher adds details: irrigation expansion increased productivity; temples were economic hubs holding donated wealth and providing credit to merchants.

Students use the writing frame to answer: 'Using three of the five institutions you have studied, explain how India's economy sustained itself across repeated political changes between the 13th and 17th centuries.' The frame prompts: Institution → what it did → why it could continue despite political changes → what it reveals about Indian society. Students write independently.

Three students read their paragraphs. Teacher consolidates: by the late 17th century, economic stress increased for common people — peasants left with little after taxes, craftspeople facing harsh conditions, warfare causing displacement. The institutions that sustained continuity did not protect everyone equally. The chapter's closing observation — that coexistence and interdependence persisted despite periodic religious clashes — is the analytical capstone.

periods.section_context: Shrenis, jatis, hundi system, temple economies, Calicut/Surat/Mangalore/Hooghly trade ports
periods.teacher_notes: The hundi system is frequently overlooked but is analytically significant — it is a sophisticated financial instrument enabling commerce without physical currency movement, which shows medieval Indian trade as far more institutionally complex than students typically assume. The temple economy section should not be treated as only religious; temples as credit providers and maritime trade funders is an economic argument. The late-17th-century deterioration in peasant and artisan conditions is important to name explicitly — it prevents the unit from becoming a celebratory account of resilience.

periods.activity_title: Faiths, Coexistence, and Conflict: Communities in Medieval India
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Short reflective essay prompt (teacher-prepared)
Peer feedback sheet: two criteria — 'Uses specific evidence' and 'Addresses both coexistence and conflict'
periods.visual_aids: Two-column board list built during discussion: 'Evidence of coexistence and inclusion' | 'Evidence of conflict and persecution'

time_bands.activity: Teacher builds the two-column list with student input: left column — Akbar's sulh-i-kul and Rajput marriage alliances, Guru Nanak's message of equality, Guru Tegh Bahadur defending Kashmiri Pandits, economic interdependence across faith communities, Ain-i-Akbari's articulation of interfaith respect; right column — jizya and pilgrimage tax, Aurangzeb's 1669 demolition orders, Guru Arjan tortured to death, periodic clashes over desecrated sacred sites. Students suggest additional entries.

Teacher asks: 'The chapter says people of different faiths largely coexisted and were economically interdependent — even while these specific conflicts occurred. Is that a contradiction, or can both be true simultaneously?' Students write a three-sentence initial response. Teacher takes three responses, does not adjudicate, and moves to the reflective essay.

Students write a reflective essay (approximately 150–200 words) responding to: 'Using specific evidence from the medieval period, explain how coexistence and conflict between communities coexisted in India between the 13th and 17th centuries. What does this tell us about the relationship between political power and community relations?' Students draft independently; teacher circulates and prompts: 'Are you explaining why these things happened together, or just listing that they did?'

Students exchange essays with a partner and apply the peer feedback sheet — marking whether specific evidence is used and whether both coexistence and conflict are addressed. Teacher closes: the chapter's position is that India's resilience across this period was expressed both through resistance and through continuing creativity — the two-column list is not a ledger of failure and success but a map of a complex social reality.

periods.section_context: Intercommunal coexistence, economic interdependence, jizya, desecrated sacred sites, sulh-i-kul legacy
periods.teacher_notes: The two-column board exercise is only productive if students draw on specific named events from across the whole chapter — not just this section — so prompt them by name: sulh-i-kul, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Aurangzeb's 1669 edict. The reflective essay should not be treated as a free-expression task; the peer feedback criteria make it an evidence-based analytical exercise. Students sometimes conflate the chapter's 'coexistence' observation with a claim that conflict did not matter — push them toward the more nuanced position that both operated simultaneously within the same social fabric.

periods.activity_title: Reshaping India's Political Map: A Chapter Synthesis
materials: Textbook Chapter 2
Large blank sheet of paper per group of four
Coloured markers
periods.visual_aids: Blank board — filled collaboratively during the session

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the chapter's organising question as a synthesis prompt: 'The chapter is called Reshaping India's Political Map. By the end of the 17th century, what had been reshaped — and what had stayed the same?' Students spend five minutes writing individually: two things that changed fundamentally, two things that persisted despite all the political upheaval. Teacher takes a quick show of hands on the most common answers to surface the range.

Groups of four receive a large sheet and create a cause-effect-continuity map of the chapter. The map must include: (1) at least three named empires or dynasties with one key change each produced; (2) at least three named resistance movements with the factor that made each possible; (3) at least two administrative systems with the social group most affected by each; (4) at least two institutions from the People's Lives section that persisted across political changes. Teacher circulates, asking: 'Have you shown a connection between two of these, not just listed them?' Groups must draw at least two arrows connecting non-obvious elements — for example, connecting the paik system to Ahom independence, or the hundi system to trade continuity despite warfare.

Each group briefly presents one non-obvious connection they drew on their map — the arrow they are most proud of — in two sentences. Other groups note whether they agree or would revise it. Teacher records the most analytically rich connections on the board, building a class-level synthesis map. Students add any connection from the board to their own maps that they had missed.

Teacher poses a final reflective question for students to answer individually in their notebooks: 'The chapter ends by saying India's resilience across this period was expressed through both military resistance and continuing creativity in art, literature, architecture, music, and spirituality. Which of these two expressions of resilience do you find more historically significant, and why? Use one specific example to support your position.' Students write — this is a take-away prompt, not assessed in this sitting.

periods.section_context: All chapter dynasties, resistance movements, administrative systems, People's Lives institutions, resilience
periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis map is productive only if groups are pushed beyond listing toward connecting — the two-arrow minimum for non-obvious connections is the key structural requirement. The final reflective question deliberately refuses a correct answer, asking students to exercise evaluative judgment rather than recall a chapter conclusion. The chapter's closing claim about resilience — military and cultural — is worth reading aloud verbatim as the session's closing frame.

For each arrow in your map, write a brief label explaining the connection.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Step 1: Choose one decision — Ala-ud-din Khilji's expansion campaigns, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's capital-shift to Daulatabad, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's copper currency experiment, or the aftermath of Timur's 1398 raid. Write it in the centre box.
Step 2: Draw two arrows outward. At the end of each, write one direct consequence — something the chapter says happened as a result of that decision.
Step 3: Choose one of your consequences and draw a further arrow from it. Write the second-order consequence at the end of that arrow.
Step 4: Label each arrow with a short phrase explaining why one thing led to the other (e.g., 'because the army needed funding' or 'because merchants lost confidence in the currency').
Step 5: Below your map, write two sentences: 'The pattern I see in this chain is...' and 'One thing that could have broken this chain is...'
format_of_output: A hand-drawn cause-effect map on paper with labelled boxes and arrows
Two written sentences below the map addressing the pattern and a possible break-point
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may use a simple linear chain (box → arrow → box) rather than a branching map; the analytical content, not the visual form, is assessed.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task asks students to operationalise causal analysis — not just name events but construct logical connections between a decision and its cascading consequences, and then identify a second-order effect. This demonstrates the LO's core demand: analysing how policy failures produce cascading social and economic consequences.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Step 1 forces a single focus decision, preventing the common error of trying to map the entire Sultanate in one diagram. Steps 2–3 build the causal chain structure. Step 4 is the analytical linchpin: the arrow labels are where students must articulate the mechanism of causation, not just sequence. Step 5 pushes from description to pattern recognition and counterfactual reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Arrow labels name a specific mechanism (e.g., 'merchants stopped accepting copper, disrupting trade'); second-order consequence is genuinely caused by the first-order consequence, not just another event from the same period; the two sentences reflect on an identifiable pattern and propose a plausible intervention. Weak: Boxes contain event names without mechanism labels on arrows; second-order consequence is unrelated to the first; sentences in Step 5 restate the decision rather than identifying a pattern.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this LO because the LO requires constructing a causal chain — the map's visual structure makes the chain's logic visible and assessable. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu (comparison table, annotated diagram, structured discussion with written output, or source analysis task) if a different format better fits the classroom context.

competency.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the structural factors — geographic, political, and organisational — that enabled communities to sustain resistance against expansionist powers.
assessment_items.question_text: The Musunuri Nayakas formed a confederacy of over 75 Telugu chieftains that successfully expelled the Delhi Sultanate's forces from Warangal around 1330–1336. Which factor most directly explains why confederacy-building was an effective strategy against the Sultanate in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: It allowed the chieftains to appeal directly to the Sultanate's sultan for negotiated terms, avoiding military confrontation entirely.

options.label: B
options.text: It gave the confederacy access to the Bahmani Sultanate's military resources, which were decisive in expelling the Delhi forces.

options.label: C
options.text: It unified fragmented local power into a collective force large enough to match or exceed what any individual chieftain could deploy against a centralised empire.

options.label: D
options.text: It was possible only because the Sultanate had already been weakened by Timur's raid, leaving its forces unable to respond effectively.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads the confederacy's purpose as diplomatic rather than military; the chapter presents it as a force that expelled Sultanate troops, not one that negotiated.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Commits a chronological error — Timur's raid occurred in 1398, several decades after the Nayakas expelled the Sultanate from Warangal in 1330–1336.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Imports an alliance with the Bahmani Sultanate that the chapter does not state; confuses two separate Deccan political entities.

competency.competency_text: Identify reasons behind harmony and conflict among social groups and communities and their impact on human societies.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare contrasting strategies of sustained resistance — martial tradition, institutional design, terrain knowledge — and evaluate their effectiveness across different political contexts.

options.label: A
options.text: Both groups relied primarily on superior cavalry forces, which the Mughals could not match due to their dependence on infantry and artillery.

options.label: B
options.text: The Ahom paik system converted land rights into a renewable military obligation, giving the state a large force without permanent maintenance costs, while the Rajputs relied on clan-based mobilisation that was effective but required ongoing leadership unity.

options.label: C
options.text: The Ahoms succeeded because they received military support from the Sikh Khalsa, which had developed a standing army by the late 17th century.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rajputs were more successful than the Ahoms because they eventually negotiated marriage alliances with the Mughals, which the Ahoms never achieved.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Group | Key resistance resource | Outcome against Mughals
Rajputs (Mewar/Marwar) | Clan-based martial tradition; Aravalli terrain; Bhil community support | Partial: some clans maintained independence; some formed marriage alliances
Ahoms (Brahmaputra Valley) | Paik system; forest/river terrain knowledge; guerrilla tactics | Near-total: defeated Mughal force of 30,000 at Saraighat (1671); preserved independence
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with the term 'paik system' may use the table's row on the Ahoms to infer its function before selecting an answer.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Treats Rajput marriage alliances as a marker of success rather than as a form of accommodation that itself signals partial Mughal dominance — misreads the chapter's framing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Fabricates a claim about Mughal military composition; the chapter does not describe the Mughals as lacking cavalry, and Babur's gunpowder advantage is from the founding of the empire, not from anti-Rajput campaigns.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents an alliance between the Ahoms and the Sikh Khalsa that the chapter does not describe; conflates two separate resistance narratives studied in different sections.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how state-directed religious persecution escalates community conflict and transforms a community's self-conception and organisation.
assessment_items.question_text: Guru Nanak founded Sikhism on the principles of equality, compassion, and belief in the oneness of God. By 1699, Guru Gobind Singh had founded the Khalsa — a martial brotherhood committed to justice and defence of faith. Explain the chain of events that transformed a community founded on spiritual principles into one with a martial organisation. Name at least two specific events in your explanation.
expected_elements: Names Guru Arjan's torture and death under Emperor Jahangir as a trigger event.
Explains Guru Hargobind's response: introducing martial training and forming a Sikh army.
Names Guru Tegh Bahadur's public execution in Delhi in 1675 on Aurangzeb's orders (for defending Kashmiri Pandits against religious persecution).
Explains Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa in 1699 as a direct response to this persecution.
Connects the transformation to escalating Mughal state action against the Sikh community, not to internal religious change alone.

competency.competency_text: Assess the influence of social, cultural, and political institutions on individuals, groups, and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess how the structural design of a revenue-administration system shapes the distribution of power and burden across different social groups.
assessment_items.question_text: The iqta system assigned territories to nobles called iqtadars, who collected taxes for the sultan's treasury — primarily to fund the army. Crucially, these posts were not hereditary. Assess: how did the non-hereditary nature of the iqta post most directly shape the experience of the peasantry?

options.label: A
options.text: Because iqtadars changed frequently, peasants benefited from lower tax rates as each new iqtadar began his tenure by building local goodwill.

options.label: B
options.text: Iqtadars, knowing their tenure was temporary, had strong incentives to extract maximum revenue as quickly as possible, placing the heaviest burden on peasants who could not appeal to a permanent local authority.

options.label: C
options.text: The non-hereditary system meant peasants could petition the sultan directly, bypassing the iqtadar and gaining protection from excessive taxation.

options.label: D
options.text: The system had no significant impact on peasants, who paid fixed rates set by the sultan regardless of which iqtadar administered the territory.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a direct-petition mechanism that the chapter does not describe; misreads the non-hereditary feature as a protection rather than a vulnerability for peasants.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the structural incentive — assumes new iqtadars prioritised goodwill over revenue extraction, which contradicts the chapter's framing of the system as army-funding centred.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Denies the iqtadar any independent role in tax collection, which contradicts the chapter's description of the system as one where iqtadars collected taxes rather than merely enforcing a central rate.

competency.competency_text: Assess the influence of social, cultural, and political institutions on individuals, groups, and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess the effectiveness of administrative reforms by comparing institutional designs and identifying persistent structural tensions in revenue and military systems.
assessment_items.question_text: Akbar's mansabdari system required officers (mansabdars) to maintain specified numbers of troops and animals according to their rank. They were paid through jagirs — land grants — and were known as jagirdars. A student argues: 'The mansabdari system solved the problems of the iqta system.' Which of the following most accurately evaluates this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is fully correct: because mansabdars were ranked by the emperor and paid set salaries, they had no reason to extract extra revenue from peasants on their jagirs.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is incorrect: the mansabdari system was less effective than the iqta system because it required a permanent standing army, which was far more expensive to maintain.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is irrelevant because the two systems operated in completely different regions and were never in direct competition with each other.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is partially correct: the mansabdari system added ranked obligations and specialised ministers, improving coordination — but jagirdars, like iqtadars, still had incentives to extract maximum revenue from their land grants.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses ranked obligation with salaried payment — the chapter states mansabdars were paid through jagirs (land grants), not fixed salaries, preserving the same extraction incentive as iqtadars.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the chapter's description: the mansabdari system explicitly avoided a permanent standing army by having mansabdars maintain their own troops — this was a feature it shared with the iqta system.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies a false geographic separation — both systems operated within overlapping north Indian imperial territories and are explicitly compared in the chapter's administrative section.

assessment_items.question_text: Todar Mal, Akbar's finance minister, introduced systematic land surveys to improve revenue collection. Explain what problem the land surveys were designed to address and assess whether this reform would have benefited peasants, the emperor, or both — and why.
expected_elements: Identifies the problem: inconsistent or arbitrarily set land revenue that did not reflect actual agricultural productivity.
Explains that systematic surveys created a data basis for revenue assessment, reducing arbitrary extraction.
Assesses the emperor's benefit: more reliable and potentially higher revenue collection based on actual land productivity.

Addresses the peasant dimension: survey-based rates could protect against arbitrary over-taxation, but the chapter also notes that non-Muslim officials remained a minority in senior posts, suggesting limits to reform reach.
Offers a judgment — 'both' or 'primarily the emperor' — supported by reasoning from the system's design, not just assertion.

competency.competency_text: Collect and interpret multiple sources of information (primary and secondary).

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract and critically assess information from a traveller's primary account to draw inferences about a historical society.
assessment_items.question_text: The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited the Vijayanagara Empire and recorded the city as remarkably prosperous and well-populated. A historian using Paes' account as a source must consider its limitations. Which of the following is the most significant limitation of Paes' account as historical evidence about Vijayanagara?

options.label: A
options.text: As a foreign visitor who likely observed mainly the capital city and its court, Paes may not have had access to conditions in rural areas, artisan communities, or regions distant from the centre of power.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Paes wrote in Portuguese, his account cannot be translated accurately into other languages, making it unusable for Indian historians.

options.label: C
options.text: Paes visited after the Battle of Talikota, so his account describes the empire after its most prosperous period had already ended.

options.label: D
options.text: Since Paes was a merchant rather than a scholar, his observations about the city's prosperity were based on prices and trade volumes rather than direct observation.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies an implausible methodological objection — translation of historical sources is standard historical practice; this reflects a misconception about how historians use non-English sources.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Commits a chronological error — Paes visited during Krishnadevaraya's reign in the early 16th century; the Battle of Talikota occurred in 1565, after Krishnadevaraya's death in 1529.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Invents a detail about Paes being a merchant that the chapter does not state; also misunderstands that direct observation is available to any visitor, regardless of profession.

competency.competency_text: Collect and interpret multiple sources of information (primary and secondary).

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret an autobiographical primary source to identify the author's perspective and distinguish it from neutral historical record.
assessment_items.question_text: The Baburnama is Babur's own autobiography, written in his own words. A student argues: 'The Baburnama is the most reliable source about Babur's campaigns because it is a first-hand account.' Identify the most significant problem with this argument.

options.label: A
options.text: An autobiography written by the subject himself is shaped by the author's own interests, self-image, and desire to justify his decisions — it is first-hand but not neutral.

options.label: B
options.text: First-hand accounts are always less reliable than secondary sources because secondary sources are written later with more complete information.

options.label: C
options.text: The Baburnama cannot be used as historical evidence because it was written to entertain the Mughal court rather than to record accurate events.

options.label: D
options.text: The Baburnama was written in a language other than the language of the territories Babur conquered, making it an external rather than an internal source.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates language of composition with source reliability — the issue is bias, not linguistic origin; this reflects a misconception about what makes a source limited.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reverses the actual methodological principle — secondary sources have their own limitations and are not automatically more reliable than first-hand accounts; this is a systematic misconception about source hierarchy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a purpose (court entertainment) that the chapter does not assign to the Baburnama; also incorrectly implies that entertainment purpose disqualifies a source as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Recognise elements of continued prevalence of certain beliefs, relationships, practices, and activities in human society notwithstanding major changes.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify which economic institutions and practices persisted across political changes and explain what made them resilient.
assessment_items.question_text: The hundi system allowed merchants to transfer funds across long distances without physically carrying currency. This system continued to operate through the rise and fall of multiple political empires between the 13th and 17th centuries. What feature of the hundi system most directly explains its persistence across political changes?

options.label: A
options.text: It required no literacy or numeracy, making it accessible to peasants and artisans who formed its primary user base across all political regimes.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a trust-based instrument operating through commercial networks that did not depend on any single political authority to function.

options.label: C
options.text: It was protected by explicit laws passed by both the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, which ensured its continuity across dynasties.

options.label: D
options.text: It was used exclusively by Muslim merchants, who maintained political connections with the ruling sultans and emperors that shielded the system from disruption.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents explicit legal protections that the chapter does not describe; misattributes the hundi's persistence to state action rather than to its independence from state authority.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Incorrectly restricts the hundi to Muslim merchants, which the chapter does not state; also misunderstands the mechanism of persistence as political protection rather than structural independence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Invents a detail about the hundi's user base and its technical requirements; the chapter describes it as a sophisticated financial instrument serving trade networks, not peasant communities.

competency.competency_text: Recognise elements of continued prevalence of certain beliefs, relationships, practices, and activities in human society notwithstanding major changes.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an argument showing how continuity in community relations persists alongside — not despite — political and religious conflict.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that 'despite periodic clashes over desecrated sacred sites, people of different faiths largely coexisted and were economically interdependent.' A student argues this claim is contradicted by Aurangzeb's 1669 demolition orders and the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Which response best evaluates this student's argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct: the chapter's claim about coexistence is disproved by Aurangzeb's policies, showing that religious conflict was the defining feature of this period.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is incorrect because Aurangzeb's policies were reversed by his successors, so they did not represent lasting religious conflict across the full period.

options.label: C
options.text: The student's examples are irrelevant because Aurangzeb's demolition orders affected only temples in Varanasi, Mathura, and Somnath, which were isolated cases with no broader social impact.

options.label: D
options.text: The student's examples show state-directed persecution, but economic interdependence and daily coexistence operated at a community level that was not fully controlled by imperial decrees — both can be true simultaneously.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Accepts the student's argument uncritically by treating state actions as equivalent to the full social reality; fails to distinguish imperial policy from community-level economic and social relations.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a claim about successors reversing Aurangzeb's policies that the chapter does not make; deflects the analytical challenge rather than engaging with the simultaneity of conflict and coexistence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Minimises the scale of Aurangzeb's demolition orders — the chapter explicitly names a broader pattern including gurudwaras — and incorrectly treats them as isolated, making this both factually and analytically wrong.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of inclusion across communities and social groups.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate specific policies and doctrines as evidence of — or departures from — traditions of inclusion in governance.
assessment_items.question_text: Akbar promoted the doctrine of sulh-i-kul ('peace with all') and established a 'house of translation' at Fatehpur Sikri where major Sanskrit texts including the Mahabharata, Ramayana, Bhagavad Gita, and Panchatantra were translated into Persian. Evaluate: what do these two actions together suggest about Akbar's approach to governing a diverse empire?

options.label: A
options.text: They suggest that Akbar converted to Hinduism, abandoning Islam as the state religion in favour of a syncretic faith he himself founded.

options.label: B
options.text: They suggest that Akbar used intellectual and doctrinal engagement with other traditions as instruments of political inclusion — legitimising Mughal rule by demonstrating respect for the empire's diverse cultural inheritance.

options.label: C
options.text: They suggest that Akbar was primarily interested in literature and had little interest in the political dimensions of religious diversity.

options.label: D
options.text: They suggest that the translation project was designed to replace Persian as the court language with Sanskrit, making the administration more accessible to Hindu subjects.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates intellectual engagement with other traditions with religious conversion; the chapter describes Akbar's interfaith dialogues and sulh-i-kul without any claim that he abandoned Islam.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Separates literary interest from political intent in a way that contradicts the chapter's framing of the translation project as part of Akbar's broader strategy of political accommodation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the direction of the translation — texts were translated from Sanskrit into Persian, meaning Persian remained the court language; this reflects a misreading of the translation project's purpose.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of inclusion across communities and social groups.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific acts and principles that exemplify cross-community solidarity and the defence of others' rights as part of a broader inclusion tradition.
assessment_items.question_text: In 1675, Guru Tegh Bahadur stood against Aurangzeb's religious persecution on behalf of Kashmiri Pandits — a Hindu community — and was publicly executed in Delhi on Aurangzeb's orders. Which principle does this act most directly exemplify?

options.label: A
options.text: Cross-community solidarity — the willingness to defend the rights and freedom of a different religious community at personal cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Military resistance — the use of armed force to protect communities from Mughal aggression.

options.label: C
options.text: Political alliance — a formal agreement between the Sikh community and Kashmiri Pandits to jointly oppose Mughal authority.

options.label: D
options.text: Religious syncretism — the merging of Sikh and Hindu beliefs into a single unified faith tradition.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses Guru Tegh Bahadur's act of solidarity with a doctrinal merging of religions; conflates inter-community defence with syncretism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Mischaracterises the act — Guru Tegh Bahadur's stand was non-violent and resulted in his execution; the martial response came from Guru Gobind Singh's subsequent founding of the Khalsa.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Imports a formal political alliance structure that the chapter does not describe; the act was individual moral solidarity, not an institutional agreement between two communities.

competency.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how trade institutions and financial instruments sustained commerce and shaped daily economic life across communities.
assessment_items.question_text: Temples in medieval India functioned as economic hubs — holding donated land and wealth, providing merchants with credit, and funding maritime trade — in addition to their religious role. Which of the following best explains why temples were able to perform these economic functions?

options.label: A
options.text: Temples accumulated large stores of donated wealth and land over generations, giving them the capital base needed to extend credit and fund trade — functions that depended on trust and accumulated resources, both of which temples had.

options.label: B
options.text: Temples employed professional merchants who managed their finances, effectively functioning as the medieval equivalent of modern commercial banks with trained staff.

options.label: C
options.text: Temples were exempt from all taxation by both the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, allowing them to reinvest their full income into trade and commerce.

options.label: D
options.text: Temples were located exclusively in port cities like Calicut and Surat, giving them direct access to maritime trade networks that other institutions lacked.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a universal tax-exemption guarantee that the chapter does not state; notably, Aurangzeb's 1669 demolition orders targeted temple property, contradicting any assumption of systematic imperial protection.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a professional merchant-staff model for temples that the chapter does not describe; the chapter presents temples as holders of donated wealth and providers of credit, not as institutionally staffed banks.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Incorrectly restricts temples to port cities — the chapter describes temples across India, including at Varanasi, Mathura, Somnath, Tirupati, and Hampi, none of which are port cities.

competency.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how trade institutions and financial instruments sustained commerce and shaped daily economic life across communities.

options.label: A
options.text: Because all four ports were located on the western coast, India had no significant trade connections with Southeast Asia or the Bay of Bengal region.

options.label: B
options.text: India imported more goods than it exported during this period, indicating that the economy was dependent on foreign production for its basic needs.

options.label: C
options.text: India's trade was structured so that high-value manufactured goods were exported while luxury and specialist imports — horses, silk — were brought in, suggesting Indian artisans and craftspeople were central to sustaining the trade balance.

options.label: D
options.text: The trade data shows that India exported horses to Central Asia in exchange for textiles, which were then distributed through the hundi system.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Port | Location | Key exports | Key imports
Calicut | Western coast (Kerala) | Textiles, spices | Horses, luxury goods
Surat | Western coast (Gujarat) | Textiles, cotton goods | Silk, luxury goods
Mangalore | Western coast (Karnataka) | Ship-built goods, weapons | Horses
Hooghly | Eastern coast (Bengal) | Textiles, utensils | Silk, luxury goods
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use the table's export and import columns to answer without requiring prior memorisation of trade details.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misreads the table — exports (textiles, weapons, ship-built goods) are manufactured goods, while imports are luxury items (silk, horses), indicating a trade surplus in manufactured goods, not dependency on foreign production.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the direction of horse trade — the chapter states India imported horses, not exported them; this reflects a specific factual confusion about a named import commodity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Incorrectly claims all four ports are on the western coast — Hooghly is on the eastern coast (Bengal), which the table's location column clearly shows; this reflects a failure to read the table carefully.
